newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai stock exchange lowers trading fees.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai stock exchange lowers trading fees.

text.p: The Shanghai stock exchange on Tuesday announced reduced trading fees and a shift to more off-floor trading in what analysts said was an effort to seize back the initiative from its fiesty competitor in Shenzhen.
Trading volume on the stock exchange in Shenzhen next to Hong Kong, which until a few months ago was languishing, is now roughly equivalent to that on the Shanghai exchange.

A spokesman for the Shanghai Stock Exchange said that from October 3 commissions on share and fund trading will be lowered to 0.35 percent from 0.4 percent. Handling charges will be lowered to 0.012 percent from 0.015 percent.
"These measures will help to further reduce the costs to investors of investing capital and to enliven the market," the Shanghai Securities News said.
An analyst with a foreign brokerage said the Shanghai exchange was under pressure from brokers to make itself more competitive.
"This is Shanghai's response to Shenzhen, which cut its fees in a similar way some time ago," the analyst said.
The exchange also announced that it would expand off-floor trading to allow securities houses and investors to trade via remote computer connections.

"While maintaining a certain number of trading-floor seats, the exchange will facilitate off-floor bidding and make such transactions the principal method of trading," the Securities News quoted an official as saying.

"A test case we have been running has proved very successful, so we will now be gradually implementing it, allowing for companies throughout China to do remote trading on the exchange," said an exchange spokesman.
"There will no longer be any need for firms to have representatives on the floor of the exchange," he added.
He said the change applied to all securities firms, both domestic and foreign, which trade on the exchange.
The Shanghai exchange has seen its position as China's premier stock market come under attack in recent months with the Shenzhen market rapidly expanding its business.

"These measures show that the Shanghai exchange is serious about boosting trading and gradually making itself China's premier financial centre," said an analyst with China Trust and Investment Co. "Right now, it's about equal with Shenzhen."

Meanwhile, the president of the Shanghai exchange, Yang Xianghai, was quoted as saying that China's securities market had entered a positive phase this year because of more policy support from the government.

Yang was quoted in the official media as saying the central government has stated more clearly than ever that it supports the securities market and has taken concrete measures to stimulate its development.
He said the Shanghai city government was giving special support to listed firms with the aim of promoting market prosperity.
Analysts say the Shenzhen market has benefitted over recent months from active support from the local city government.
